sections.overview: The Eurasian wren is a tiny, round songbird and one of the most numerous breeding birds in Britain. It is often heard before it is seen: a male defends his territory with a song far louder than his body size suggests.
sections.identification: An adult weighs about 10 g and has a wing length near 49 mm. The plumage is brown with dark barring on the wings, tail and underparts, a pale stripe above the eye and a paler throat. The short tail is often held upright. The sexes look alike; juveniles are darker.
sections.habitat: In Britain it is most frequent in deciduous woodland, but it also lives in scrub, pastoral farmland, villages, towns and conifer woods. It favours dense vegetation close to the ground, where it forages and finds nest sites.
sections.diet: The wren forages mostly on the ground, picking up insects and their larvae, spiders and millipedes. Beside water it may also take aquatic invertebrates.
sections.behavior: Males use song to establish and defend territories, often singing from low perches. A male also builds several domed nests of moss, grass and twigs, frequently in holes; these are known as cock nests.
sections.reproduction: In Britain, laying begins on average in early May. A clutch is typically five or six eggs, incubated by the female for 16–18 days. The chicks are downy and helpless, and fledge after roughly 14.5–18 days. The female usually raises the brood. Breeding typically starts at one year of age.
sections.ecology: Wrens help regulate insect populations and are themselves prey for domestic cats and for birds such as jays and magpies; crows and jays also raid nests. The common cuckoo sometimes parasitises wren nests.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern. The UK breeding population was estimated at 11 million territories in 2016 and has risen by 127% since 1967, though numbers fall after severe winters and then recover. A wren typically lives about two years; the oldest recorded in Britain reached over seven.
